lead: Some rankings decide every pair: given two numbers, either one is smaller or the other is. Other rankings leave gaps — 4 does not divide 6, and 6 does not divide 4. A partial order ranks elements while allowing such incomparable pairs, and the pair (set, partial order) is called a poset. A Hasse diagram draws only the links that cannot be skipped, so every implied comparison disappears. Posets order build steps in a compiler, subclasses in a class hierarchy, and versions in a repository.
prereq: You need: reflexivity, antisymmetry and transitivity from Chapter 2.2, plus the contrast with Chapter 2.4.

blocks.text: A relation R on a set A is a partial order when three properties hold. Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for every a in A. Antisymmetric: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R together force a = b. Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R together force (a, c) ∈ R. For such an R we write a ≼ b instead of (a, b) ∈ R, read it as 'a is below b', and call the pair (A, ≼) a poset.

The word partial is the point. In the divisibility poset ({1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12}, |), where a | b means a divides b, we get 2 ≼ 6, yet 4 and 6 are unrelated: neither divides the other. Two elements that the order does compare are comparable. When every pair is comparable — a ≼ b or b ≼ a, always — the order is total, and the poset is a chain.

items: ≤ on the real numbers is a total order.
Divisibility on the positive integers is partial: 4 and 6 are incomparable.
⊆ on the power set P(S) is partial: {1} and {2} are incomparable.

blocks.text: A subset whose elements are pairwise incomparable is an antichain. In the divisibility poset, {4, 6} is an antichain and so is {2, 3}.

Transitivity means many related pairs carry no new information. The covering relation keeps only the essential ones: b covers a when a ≺ b and no c satisfies a ≺ c ≺ b. Here 4 covers 2, but 12 does not cover 2, because 4 lies strictly between.

items: Arrange elements so that a ≺ b puts b above a.
Remove every self-loop, which reflexivity would repeat.
Replace each arrow by a plain line; upward now means greater.
Remove any line already forced by transitivity — 1–12 goes, because 1–2–4–12 exists.

blocks.text: The result is the Hasse diagram. To read it, follow upward paths: a ≼ b holds exactly when an upward path runs from a to b. No path in either direction means the two elements are incomparable.

A maximal element has nothing above it: no b with a ≺ b. A minimal element has nothing below it. Several of each may exist. In {2, 3, 4, 6} under divisibility, 4 and 6 are maximal and 2 and 3 are minimal.

A greatest element g satisfies x ≼ g for every x, and a least element l satisfies l ≼ x for every x. These are stronger demands, and a poset may have neither. When they exist they are unique, by antisymmetry.

For a subset B of A, an upper bound is an element u with b ≼ u for every b in B; a lower bound is an element l with l ≼ b for every b. The least upper bound (LUB, supremum) is the smallest upper bound; the greatest lower bound (GLB, infimum) is the largest lower bound. In A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} under divisibility, for B = {4, 6} the only upper bound is 12, so LUB = 12; the lower bounds are 1 and 2, so GLB = 2. In the smaller poset {2, 3, 4, 6}, {4, 6} has no upper bound and only the lower bound 2.

A poset is well ordered when every nonempty subset has a least element; the positive integers under ≤ are the standard case. Reversing every comparison, a ≼' b exactly when b ≼ a, gives the dual poset, which is again a partial order.

figure.caption: Only covering pairs are drawn: the link 1 to 12 is implied by 1–2–4–12, so it is left out.

spec.aria: Hasse diagram of {1,2,3,4,6,12} under divisibility, with 1 at the bottom, 12 at the top, and a line joining each element to the elements it covers.

examples.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12} and define a R b to mean a divides b. (i) Show that (A, R) is a poset. (ii) List the covering pairs and describe the Hasse diagram. (iii) Find the maximal, minimal, greatest and least elements, and decide whether R is a total order. (iv) Find the LUB and GLB of {4, 6}.
steps: Reflexive: every a satisfies a | a, because a = 1 × a. All 6 elements pass.
Antisymmetric: if a | b and b | a with a and b positive, then a = b.
Transitive: if b = a·k and c = b·m, then c = a·(k·m), so a | c.
All three properties hold, so R is a partial order and (A, R) is a poset.
Covering pairs: (1,2), (1,3), (2,4), (2,6), (3,6), (4,12), (6,12) — that is 7 pairs. The pair (2,12) is skipped because 4 and 6 lie strictly between.
Hasse diagram: 1 at the bottom, 2 and 3 in the second row, 4 and 6 in the third, 12 at the top. No line joins 1 to 12.
Maximal: only 12, since no element of A is a proper multiple of 12. It lies above every element, so it is also the greatest element.
Minimal: only 1, since no element other than 1 divides 1. It lies below every element, so it is also the least element.
Total order? No. 4 and 6 are incomparable, so the poset is not a chain.
Upper bounds of {4, 6}: elements x with 4 | x and 6 | x, giving x = 12 only. So LUB = 12. Lower bounds: elements x with x | 4 and x | 6, giving 1 and 2, so GLB = 2.
The height of a poset is the number of elements in its longest chain (some books call the number of edges the length and count one less). Here 1 ≺ 2 ≺ 4 ≺ 12 has 4 elements, so the height is 4.
examples.answer: R is a partial order with 7 covering pairs; 12 is the greatest and only maximal element, 1 is the least and only minimal element, 4 and 6 are incomparable so R is not a total order, and LUB{4,6} = 12 while GLB{4,6} = 2.
examples.check:
A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12]
R = [(a, b) for a in A for b in A if b % a == 0]
refl = all((a, a) in R for a in A)
anti = all(a == b for (a, b) in R if (b, a) in R)
trans = all((a, c) in R for (a, b) in R for (b2, c) in R if b == b2)
print(int(refl and anti and trans))
cov = [(a, b) for (a, b) in R if a != b and not any((a, c) in R and (c, b) in R for c in A if c != a and c != b)]
print(len(cov))
print(max(b for b in A if not any(b != c and (b, c) in R for c in A)))
print(min(a for a in A if not any(a != c and (c, a) in R for c in A)))
ub = [b for b in A if (4, b) in R and (6, b) in R]
print(min(ub))
lb = [a for a in A if (a, 4) in R and (a, 6) in R]
print(max(lb))
def height(x):
    below = [y for y in A if (y, x) in R and y != x]
    return 1 + max((height(y) for y in below), default=0)
print(max(height(a) for a in A))

traps: Drawing a line for every related pair: 1–12, 1–6 and 2–12 all appear, and the diagram stops being a Hasse diagram.
Stopping at '12 is maximal' — maximal and greatest are different words, and 12 is both only because this poset has a single maximal element.
Assuming a least or greatest element always exists: {2, 3, 4, 6} under divisibility has neither.
Treating any upper bound as the LUB. Several upper bounds can exist, and only the smallest one is the LUB.
Reading a Hasse diagram as a digraph with missing arrows: direction is upward only, and a line means the lower element is below the upper one.

quiz.q: State the three properties that make a relation a partial order, with the formal condition for each.
quiz.a: Reflexive: (a, a) ∈ R for all a. Antisymmetric: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, a) ∈ R force a = b. Transitive: (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R force (a, c) ∈ R.

quiz.q: Which three kinds of information does a Hasse diagram remove from the digraph of a partial order?
quiz.a: Self-loops, arrowheads (plain lines replace arrows), and lines already implied by transitivity.

quiz.q: Why is divisibility on {2, 3, 6} not a total order, and which elements form an antichain there?
quiz.a: 2 divides 6 and 3 divides 6, but neither 2 nor 3 divides the other, so they are incomparable. The set {2, 3} is an antichain.

quiz.q: Explain why a greatest element, when it exists, is unique and is the only maximal element.
quiz.a: If g and g′ are both above every element, then g ≼ g′ and g′ ≼ g, so g = g′ by antisymmetry. Nothing can lie above g, so no other element is maximal.

quiz.q: On A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} under divisibility, find the LUB and GLB of {2, 3}.
quiz.a: Upper bounds are multiples of both 2 and 3: only 6, so LUB = 6. Lower bounds divide both: only 1, so GLB = 1.

quiz.q: Draw the Hasse diagram of P({a, b}) under ⊆ and count its covering pairs.
quiz.a: Elements ∅, {a}, {b}, {a, b}. Covering pairs are ∅–{a}, ∅–{b}, {a}–{a, b}, {b}–{a, b}: 4 lines, forming a square with ∅ at the bottom and {a, b} at the top.

quiz.q: In the poset {2, 3, 4, 6} under divisibility, a student claims a least element exists. Check the claim and list all maximal elements.
quiz.a: Minimal elements are 2 and 3, so no element lies below both and there is no least element. Maximal elements are 4 and 6, so there is no greatest element either.

beyond: Not for the exam. Build systems such as make and cargo read a dependency poset and emit a topological order, which is Unit 6 material. Dilworth's theorem says the fewest chains needed to cover a finite poset equals the size of its largest antichain. Version-control ancestry, database query planners and formal concept analysis all lean on the covering-pair idea. Search 'topological sort', 'Dilworth theorem' and 'domain theory' to go further.
